entities.summary:
Ferenc Frangepán (Latin: Franciscus Frankapan) was a highly influential Croatian nobleman, prelate, and humanist diplomat who served as Bishop of Eger (1526–1543) and later Archbishop of Kalocsa (1530–1543). Born into the powerful Frankopan family, one of Croatia's oldest and most distinguished noble houses, Frangepán emerged as a pivotal figure in the tumultuous political and religious landscape of 16th-century Central Europe, primarily known for his tireless diplomatic efforts to forge alliances against the encroaching Ottoman Empire and his patronage of Renaissance humanism. His career spanned the critical decades following the Battle of Mohács in 1526, profoundly shaping the ecclesiastical and diplomatic relations between the Hungarian Kingdom, the Habsburg Monarchy, and the Holy See.

Frangepán's ecclesiastical and political ascendancy began with his appointment as Bishop of Eger in 1526, a strategic diocese in northern Hungary. His diplomatic acumen quickly became evident as he undertook numerous missions to Rome, Venice, and other European courts, advocating for a united Christian front against the Ottoman threat, which had devastated much of Hungary. In 1530, he was elevated to Archbishop of Kalocsa, one of the two most senior ecclesiastical positions in the Hungarian Kingdom, further cementing his influence. He played a significant role in the complex succession disputes following King Louis II's death at Mohács, navigating between Ferdinand I of Habsburg and John Zápolya, while consistently prioritizing the defense of Christian Europe.

entities.summary:
Ferenc Frangepán was a Hungarian nobleman and Latinist who played a crucial role in the preservation of classical knowledge during the tumultuous 16th century. 
Born in Modruš, Croatia in 1490, Frangepán's family had long been associated with the Hungarian nobility, but it was his own intellectual pursuits that would set him apart from his contemporaries.

As a prominent Latinist and scholar of classical languages, Frangepán was instrumental in translating and preserving ancient texts, including works by Cicero and Virgil. His efforts helped to ensure the continuation of classical learning during a period marked by significant cultural upheaval.

Frankopan's legacy extends beyond his own lifetime, as his work laid the groundwork for future generations of scholars and intellectuals. Today, Frangepán is recognized as one of the most important figures in Hungarian intellectual history, and his contributions to the preservation of classical knowledge continue to be celebrated.

The passing of Ferenc Frangepán on February 7, 1543, marked the end of an era, but his impact on the world of learning would endure for centuries to come.
